reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Onset is in the neonatal period or first weeks of life with erratic, fragmentary myoclonus that migrates over different body parts, often followed by focal seizures and later tonic spasms
The EEG shows a burst-suppression pattern that is frequently more pronounced during sleep
Inborn errors of metabolism, especially non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia and other neurotransmitter or organic acid disorders, are characteristic underlying causes
Development is profoundly impaired from onset and seizures are typically refractory
It is distinguished from Ohtahara syndrome mainly by the predominant erratic myoclonus and the metabolic rather than structural aetiology
A systematic metabolic and genetic workup is essential to identify a potentially treatable cause
Vitamin-responsive epilepsies should be excluded early with therapeutic trials
reference.pathophysiology: Early myoclonic encephalopathy is a neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy strongly linked to inborn errors of metabolism, particularly non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia. Accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites and disturbance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission in the immature brain produce marked cortical and subcortical hyperexcitability. This generates erratic fragmentary myoclonus and the burst-suppression pattern, while the underlying metabolic derangement causes the severe and early developmental impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia and other inborn errors of metabolism
additionalInvestigations: EEG showing burst-suppression, often accentuated in sleep
Comprehensive metabolic screen including plasma and CSF amino acids and glycine
Trials of vitamin-responsive treatments such as pyridoxine
Epilepsy and metabolic gene panels or exome sequencing
Brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
redFlags: Refractory neonatal myoclonus with burst-suppression suggesting a metabolic encephalopathy
Elevated CSF glycine indicating non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia
Rapid clinical deterioration pointing to a progressive metabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally very poor with high early mortality and profound neurodevelopmental disability in survivors, largely determined by the underlying metabolic disorder. Seizures are usually refractory to antiseizure medication.
pitfalls: Failing to send CSF and plasma glycine to detect non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia
Not trialling vitamin-responsive therapies before concluding refractoriness
Confusing erratic myoclonus with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus
Attributing seizures to structural causes without a full metabolic workup
management: Undertake an urgent metabolic and genetic workup with empirical vitamin trials of pyridoxine, pyridoxal phosphate and folinic acid to identify a treatable cause
Treat the underlying inborn error of metabolism where identified, for example measures for non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia such as sodium benzoate and dextromethorphan
Use antiseizure medication for seizure control while recognising that seizures are frequently refractory
Provide supportive neonatal and paediatric care including feeding support, respiratory monitoring and developmental input
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given the heritable metabolic aetiologies
Involve paediatric neurology and metabolic specialists early to guide diagnosis, treatment and prognosis
Introduce palliative care discussions given the generally poor prognosis and high early mortality
